name: Tintal
story: 16 beats, four vibhags, one of the most common cycles in Hindustani music. The khali on beat 9 is the moment everything relaxes before returning home.

name: Dadra
story: A gentle 6-beat cycle that lilts like a waltz — the signature groove of thumri, bhajans, and romantic Bollywood ballads.

name: Rupak Tal
story: Rupak is unusual — the first beat (sam) is actually a khali (empty) stroke. The cycle starts weak and resolves inward.

name: Ektal
story: 12 beats, six vibhags. At vilambit tempo each beat becomes a canvas — the master tabla player elaborates endlessly between the landmarks.

name: Jhaptal
story: 10 beats grouped 2+3+2+3 — the same skeleton as Ottoman Curcuna, but arrived at through a completely different tradition.

name: Keherwa
story: The most common tala in Indian light music — bhajans, ghazals, qawwalis, and half the Bollywood catalogue rest on this 8-beat foundation.

name: Deepchandi
story: A majestic 14-beat tala for thumri and romantic classical forms — the alternating 3+4 grouping creates a long, lilting rocking cycle.

name: Chautal
story: The 12-beat cycle of dhrupad — India's oldest surviving classical vocal form, played on the thunderous pakhawaj rather than tabla.

name: Adi Tala
story: The most common Carnatic tala — "adi" means "first" or "primary." 8 beats: laghu, drutam, drutam. The bedrock of South Indian classical music.

name: Khanda Chapu
story: "Khanda" means five. A 5-beat Carnatic tala grouped 2+1+2 — uneven, with a distinctive hop at the single-beat middle.

name: Sultaal
story: 10 beats in five equal vibhags of 2 — a martial, processional cousin to Jhaptal. The perfect symmetry gives Sultaal the grandeur of Dhrupad.

name: Dhamar
story: 14 beats grouped 5+2+3+4 — the tala of Dhamar songs celebrating Krishna playing Holi. The stumbling asymmetry captures the joyful chaos of the festival of colors.

name: Addha (Drut Tintal)
story: Tintal at breakneck speed. The bols shorten to "Dha Dhi Ta Dha" — crisp syllables that articulate cleanly as singer and tabla trade virtuosic volleys.

name: Jhumra
story: A rare 14-beat Hindustani tala shaped like Deepchandi (3+4+3+4) but stretched glacially slow — each matra breathes for seconds, giving the vocalist endless space to ornament.

name: Tilwada
story: A 16-beat cousin of Tintal — same vibhag skeleton but the theka is denser, filled with connecting strokes. The tabla breathes between the singer's long-held notes.

name: Teevra
story: A 7-beat pakhawaj tala grouped 3+2+2. "Teevra" means sharp or intense — the asymmetry lends dhrupad compositions a bracing, forward lean.

name: Punjabi Tal
story: A 16-beat tala at home in Sikh kirtan and Punjabi light classical. Brisker and more insistent than Tintal, with the syncopated lean of Punjab's folk heritage.

name: Misra Chapu
story: "Misra" means mixed — tisra (3) blended with chatusra (2+2). Kept with waves only, the tala floats in suspension, a hypnotic lilt beloved in Bharatanatyam choreography.

name: Rupaka Tala
story: The second most common Carnatic tala after Adi. Drutam (1) plus laghu (2) creates a brisk triple-time cycle — the engine behind many Tyagaraja kritis.

name: Eka Tala
story: "Eka" means one — a single laghu of 4 counts. The shortest Carnatic tala, used for devotional songs and learning exercises where the cycle turns over every bar.

name: Konnakol · Ta-Ka-Di-Mi
story: Chatusra gati — four syllables per beat. "Ta-Ka-Di-Mi" is the default subdivision of Carnatic music, spoken, clapped, and drummed as the foundation of all rhythmic training.

name: Konnakol · Ta-Ki-Ta
story: Tisra gati — three syllables per beat. "Ta-Ki-Ta" is the triplet engine of Carnatic music, the gateway to polyrhythmic math and the lilting swing of South Indian groove.

name: Bhangra · Chaal
story: The thunderous dhol groove of Punjab. "Chaal" means walk — dagga heavy stick on the bass head, tilli thin stick on the treble. The half-time feel sounds faster as the dance accelerates.

name: Garba
story: Danced in concentric circles around a clay lamp during the nine nights of Navratri. The tempo builds through the night — UNESCO inscribed Garba as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2023.

name: Dandiya Raas
story: The late-night escalation of Garba — partners face off striking decorated sticks in a "ta-ta, ta-ta-ta" pattern. Pure exhilaration as the circles break into partner formations.

name: Lavani
story: Maharashtra's galloping dholki rhythm for Lavani — poetry, song, and dance fused. Ankle bells (ghungroo) interlock with the drum while the performer spins relentlessly.

name: Kalbelia
story: The sinuous Rajasthani dance of the Kalbeliya community — movement mimics the serpent. UNESCO-listed. The pungi (snake-charmer's pipe) sings over a dholak driving in uneven accents.

name: Qawwali
story: The propulsive Sufi devotional groove of the shrines — Keherwa tala driven hard, with group handclaps riding the 2 and 4. Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan carried this rhythm to the world.

name: Bollywood · Classic 4/4
story: The timeless Bollywood groove from the golden era through today — Keherwa tala stretched into a punchy, cinematic 16-step pattern that carries half the Hindi film catalogue.

name: Rajasthani Manganiar
story: The hereditary Manganiar musicians of the Thar Desert — dholak pulse underneath the shimmering clack of khartal wooden castanets. Centuries of Rajput patronage, now a global concert tradition.

name: Dhamaal
story: The ecstatic Sufi dhol rhythm of the shrines — associated with Shah Hussain's urs in Lahore. Devotees spin themselves into trance as the dhol's heavy stick drives the circle harder and harder.

name: Ghoomar
story: The Rajput women's spinning dance — wide circular steps in flowing skirts, performed at weddings and festivals. Elegant and graceful where Bhangra is thunderous.

name: Rupaka Chapu
story: Rupaka Chapu is the hand-waved form of Rupaka — two waves and a clap across 6 sub-beats. Ubiquitous in Tyagaraja kritis and bhajan accompaniment; faster and lighter than the full 3-beat laghu form.

name: Adi Tala · 4 Kalai
story: Adi tala stretched to 4-kalai — each of the 8 beats expanded into 4 subunits, giving 32 matras per cycle. The vilambit canvas of South Indian ragam-tanam-pallavi exploration.

name: Sankeerna Chapu
story: "Sankeerna" means compound of 4+5 or 4+2+3. The rarest of the chapu talas — a 9-beat asymmetric cycle that tilts forward then resolves into a settled close.

name: Tisra Jati Chapu
story: A 3-beat chapu — the smallest of the hand-waved cycles. Pulse is wave-wave-clap in tisra feel, lending Bharatanatyam sequences a propulsive triplet lift.

name: Adi Tala · Tisra Gati
story: Adi tala reshaped into tisra gati — 8 beats × 3 subdivisions = 24 matras. The Carnatic equivalent of a permanent triplet swing over the same foundational cycle.

name: Adi Tala · Khanda Gati
story: Adi tala in khanda gati — 8 beats × 5 subdivisions = 40 aksharas. Five syllables per beat ("Ta Di Ki Na Tom") produce a rhythmic tension with no parallel in Western meter.

name: Adi Tala · Misra Gati
story: Adi in misra gati — 8 beats × 7 aksharas = 56 subdivisions. The virtuoso's playground: konnakol syllables "Ta Ka Di Mi Ta Ki Ta" loop seven-deep per beat.

name: Baul
story: The wandering Bauls of Bengal sing with dubki hand-drum, one-string ektara, and ankle bells — a rejection of caste and creed in song. UNESCO Masterpiece of Oral Heritage (2005).

name: Baul · 6/8
story: The meditative 6/8 Baul sway — the dubki rocks while the ektara drone holds steady. A Lalon Shah song in this feel opens into timelessness.

name: Qaida · Delhi Theme
story: A kayda is the spine of modern tabla solo — a theme stated on "dha" strokes, then permuted endlessly through open/closed bayan variants. This is the Delhi gharana's template, the grammar every gharana inherits.

name: Peshkar · Tabla Opening
story: The opening movement of a tabla solo. Peshkar means "to present" — the artist unveils the tala's character slowly, stating themes that may never fully establish before transforming. A musical invocation.

name: Tihai · Sam Landing
story: A tihai is a phrase repeated three times so the last stroke lands precisely on sam. 5 matras × 3 = 15, plus the arrival = 16. The mathematical inevitability of resolution made audible.

name: Rela · Fast Tabla
story: The rela shares the kayda's structure but runs at breakneck tempo — a continuous torrent of bols, a test of stamina and clarity. The Farrukhabad gharana lives for this moment.

name: Gat · Lucknow Composition
story: The gat is a fixed tabla composition from the Lucknow gharana — Kathak dance's rhythmic partner. The open-palm bolder strokes evoke the bells on the dancer's ankles.

name: Matta Tal
story: A rare 9-beat Hindustani pakhawaj tala grouped 2+2+2+3. The last vibhag swells by a matra, giving dhrupad compositions a long inhale before the return to sam.
